title: Given an integer array and an integer K, return the K most frequent elements. The answer may be in any order and the algorithm should be better than O(n log n) where possible.
shortTitle: Top K Frequent Elements — HashMap Frequency Plus Min-Heap or Bucket Sort

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the top K frequent elements first counts occurrences with a HashMap, then selects the K highest-frequency keys using either a size-K min-heap in O(n log K) time or bucket sort by frequency in O(n) time. The bucket approach exploits that any frequency is between one and n, so we place elements into frequency-indexed buckets and read from the high-frequency end.
s1_definition.analogy: The bank wants the K most common transaction amounts of the day. First a clerk tallies how many times each amount occurred. Then, to pick the top K, he either keeps a small shortlist of size K that always drops the least frequent when it overflows, or he lines up amounts in buckets labeled by their frequency count and reads off the buckets from the busiest end.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count frequencies in a map, then pick the top K with a size-K min-heap or with frequency buckets.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the top K frequent elements first counts occurrences with a HashMap, then selects the K highest-frequency keys using either a size-K min-heap in O(n log K) time or bucket sort by frequency in O(n) time. The bucket approach exploits that any frequency is between one and n, so we place elements into frequency-indexed buckets and read from the high-frequency end.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The bank wants the K most common transaction amounts of the day. First a clerk tallies how many times each amount occurred. Then, to pick the top K, he either keeps a small shortlist of size K that always drops the least frequent when it overflows, or he lines up amounts in buckets labeled by their frequency count and reads off the buckets from the busiest end.

**One line to remember:** Count frequencies in a map, then pick the top K with a size-K min-heap or with frequency buckets.

sections.s2_technical:
Step one is always the same: build a frequency map. For example, `Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>(); for (int x : nums) freq.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum);`.

The min-heap approach keeps a heap of size K ordered by frequency, smallest frequency on top. We iterate the map entries and offer each into the heap; when the heap exceeds K we poll the smallest. For example, `PriorityQueue<Integer> heap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> freq.get(a) - freq.get(b)); for (int key : freq.keySet()) { heap.offer(key); if (heap.size() > K) heap.poll(); }`. At the end the heap holds the K most frequent. This is O(n log K), which beats a full sort when K is much smaller than n.

The bucket-sort approach is O(n). We create an array of buckets indexed by frequency, from 0 to n, where bucket[f] is a list of elements that occurred exactly f times. We fill it from the frequency map, then walk the buckets from the highest index downward, collecting elements until we have K. Since the maximum possible frequency is n, the bucket array is size n plus one, and the whole thing is linear.

A senior-level nuance is the trade-off. The heap is simpler and streaming-friendly and ideal when K is small; the bucket sort is asymptotically optimal at O(n) but uses an array of size n plus one and is best when K can be large relative to distinct elements. Knowing when to pick which is the mark of maturity.

Another nuance is comparator correctness in the heap: ordering by frequency ascending so that the smallest-frequency element sits at the top and gets evicted when the heap overflows, which is what keeps the K largest.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants the top K most frequent transaction amounts in a day to populate a quick-select menu of common amounts for tellers. The data is a large array of amounts, and we want the K busiest values. This is exactly the top-K-frequent-elements problem.

Problem 2 — A full sort by frequency would be n-log-n, but since K is usually small, like the top five amounts, a size-K min-heap gives n-log-K, which is noticeably faster, and we present that as the primary solution.

Problem 3 — We also note the bucket-sort linear alternative for when K could be large, choosing based on the expected K relative to the number of distinct amounts.

In the code: a `FrequencyService` has a `topKFrequent` method using the size-K min-heap. A `TopKDemo` main finds the top K amounts in a sample array.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: amounts 500, 1000, 500, 2000, 1000, 500, 3000, 1000, 2000 and K equals 2.

Step 1 (count): the frequency map becomes 500 appears 3 times, 1000 appears 3 times, 2000 appears 2 times, 3000 appears 1 time.

Step 2 (heap): we offer each key into the min-heap ordered by frequency. Offer 500 (freq 3), heap has 500. Offer 1000 (freq 3), heap has 500, 1000. Offer 2000 (freq 2), heap size becomes 3, exceeds K equals 2, so poll the smallest frequency, which is 2000 (freq 2), leaving 500 and 1000. Offer 3000 (freq 1), size 3, poll smallest which is 3000, leaving 500 and 1000.

Step 3 (extract): the heap holds 500 and 1000, both frequency 3. We poll them into the result. The top 2 amounts are 500 and 1000.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26 23:30:00 [INFO] Finding the top 2 most frequent transaction amounts
2026-10-26 23:30:00 [INFO] Top K amounts -> [500, 1000]
```

```
  {500:3, 1000:3, 2000:2, 3000:1}

  offer 500,1000 → heap{500,1000}
  offer 2000 → size 3 → poll 2000
  offer 3000 → size 3 → poll 3000
  heap = {500, 1000}
    │
    ▼
  Output: top-2 amounts = [500, 1000]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the top K frequent elements is a two-stage problem. The first stage is always the same: I count how often each element appears using a HashMap. The interesting choice is the second stage, selecting the K highest-frequency keys. My primary approach is a size-K min-heap ordered by frequency with the smallest frequency on top. I offer each distinct key into the heap, and whenever the heap grows beyond K I evict the element at the top, which is the least frequent so far. After processing every key, the heap holds exactly the K most frequent elements, and this runs in n-log-K time, which is meaningfully faster than a full sort when K is small compared to n.

I also keep the bucket-sort alternative ready, which is asymptotically optimal at linear time. Because any element's frequency is between one and the array length, I can place elements into buckets indexed by their frequency and then read from the highest-frequency bucket downward until I have collected K. The trade-off is clear: the heap is simpler and ideal when K is small, while the bucket sort is linear and better when K can be large relative to the number of distinct elements, and knowing which to pick for a given workload is part of the answer.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this to compute the top K most frequent transaction amounts in a day so the teller app can present a quick-select menu of common amounts. In practice K is small, often the top five, so the size-K min-heap is the natural fit and keeps the computation fast even over a large day's worth of transactions.

The detail I always get right is the heap comparator. I order it by frequency ascending so the least frequent element sits at the top and is the one evicted when the heap overflows, which is precisely what preserves the K most frequent. Reversing that comparator by mistake would evict the wrong elements and return the least frequent instead of the most frequent, so being deliberate about the ordering direction is essential.
